title: C#: ASP.NET Core, EF Core, testing, outbound calls, auth, logging, workers and JSON (topics 15-26)
_note: rv2 S2 (PLAN §2.2 fund-cs-web row). Scope = Fundamentals C# topic gates 15-26: the six binding-list topics 15-20 plus the rv2 C7 topics 21-23 (S2b appended one idea each) and the rv3 W6 topics 24-26 (one idea each). Topic 16 (routing) has no row of its own on the binding list. Server-local side file, never stamped.

ideas.idea: Pick each service's lifetime on purpose (singleton, scoped, transient), and never let a longer-lived service hold a shorter-lived one: that is a captive dependency.
ideas.why: A singleton that captures a scoped DbContext shares one context across every request and thread, which corrupts change tracking and leaks data between users.
ideas.prompt: A singleton cache service takes AppDbContext in its constructor. It works in tests, then production shows 'a second operation was started on this context' errors and occasionally another user's data. Explain and fix.
ideas.answer: The singleton is built once, so the scoped context it captured lives for the whole app and is used by many requests at once. Inject IServiceScopeFactory or IDbContextFactory and create a short-lived context per operation, or make the cache scoped. Scope validation in development reports this mistake at startup.

ideas.idea: Middleware runs in the order it is registered, inbound and then outbound, so order is behaviour: exception handling first, routing before authentication and authorization.
ideas.why: An exception handler registered late cannot catch errors from earlier middleware, and authorization placed before routing cannot see the endpoint's policy.
ideas.prompt: In Program.cs the order is UseAuthorization, UseRouting, then UseExceptionHandler. Endpoints marked [Authorize] are reachable anonymously, and some errors return a raw stack trace page. Reorder it and explain.
ideas.answer: Put UseExceptionHandler first so it wraps everything after it. Then UseRouting, so the endpoint and its metadata are selected, then UseAuthentication and UseAuthorization, which read that metadata to enforce [Authorize]. Each middleware only sees what earlier middleware produced and only catches what runs inside it.

ideas.idea: Validate the bound model before any work and answer failures with ProblemDetails: a standard body naming the status, the problem and each invalid field.
ideas.why: Ad-hoc error bodies force every client to parse a different shape, and unvalidated models fail deep inside the service as a 500.
ideas.prompt: A signup endpoint returns 500 with a NullReferenceException when the password is missing, and a custom { error: 'bad' } body when the email is malformed. What should it return instead?
ideas.answer: Validate the request model at the edge (data annotations or a validator; [ApiController] does it automatically) and return 400 with a ValidationProblemDetails body that lists each field and its message. Use the same ProblemDetails shape for other errors, so clients read status, title and detail the same way everywhere.

ideas.idea: A DbContext is a short-lived, scoped unit of work: it tracks the entities it loaded and writes their detected changes when you call SaveChanges.
ideas.why: Without that model, updates to detached objects silently do nothing, two loads of one row surprise you by being the same instance, and long-lived contexts grow stale.
ideas.prompt: A service builds a new Customer object with an existing Id from a request body, sets its Name and calls SaveChanges. Nothing is updated and no error is raised. Explain what EF Core saw.
ideas.answer: The new object was never attached, so the context is not tracking it and SaveChanges finds no changes to write. Load the entity through the context and change the loaded instance, or attach the object and mark it modified on purpose. The context writes only what it tracks.

ideas.idea: For read-only queries, project to the shape you need with Select and use AsNoTracking; load related data in the query, never inside a loop.
ideas.why: Tracking everything you only display costs memory and time, and touching a navigation per row turns one list into hundreds of queries.
ideas.prompt: An orders page loads 200 orders with their customers by looping and calling the customer lookup per order. The SQL log shows 201 queries and memory climbs. Rewrite the query.
ideas.answer: Issue one query: context.Orders.AsNoTracking() with a Select that pulls the order fields and the customer name you display, so EF builds a single SQL join and returns plain objects. If related entities are needed in full, Include them, or load all their ids in one query, instead of one query per row.

ideas.idea: One SaveChanges call commits its changes in one transaction; work split across several SaveChanges calls needs an explicit transaction to stay all-or-nothing.
ideas.why: Two separate saves can leave half the work committed when the second one fails, such as money debited but never credited.
ideas.prompt: A transfer debits one account and calls SaveChanges, then credits the other and calls SaveChanges again. The second save fails on a concurrency check. What state is left, and how do you fix it?
ideas.answer: The debit is committed and the credit is not, so money has disappeared. Make both changes and call SaveChanges once, which wraps them in a single transaction, or open an explicit transaction around both saves and commit only after the second. Map the concurrency failure to a retry or a conflict response.

ideas.idea: Test endpoints through the real pipeline in memory and replace only the edges: whatever leaves the process, and the clock.
ideas.why: Mocking routing, validation or queries proves nothing about what clients will see, while a real email sender or clock makes tests slow, flaky or impossible to pin.
ideas.prompt: A team's endpoint tests call controller methods directly with every dependency mocked. They pass, yet a broken [Authorize] policy and a JSON casing change both reached production. What should the tests look like?
ideas.answer: Host the app with WebApplicationFactory and send real HTTP requests, so routing, binding, validation, authorization and serialization all run. In ConfigureTestServices remove and replace only the outbound senders and the TimeProvider, keep a real database engine, and assert on status codes, bodies and what the fakes recorded.

ideas.idea: Give every outbound call a timeout inside your caller's deadline, and retry only transient failures of requests that are safe to repeat, with jittered backoff and a budget.
ideas.why: An unbounded call ties up requests for the 100-second default, and blind retries charge customers twice, add latency on 4xx answers and multiply load during an outage.
ideas.prompt: An order service calls payments with a default HttpClient and retries every failure three times at once. During a payments brownout, orders hang for minutes and some customers are charged twice. What changes?
ideas.answer: Set a timeout below the order request's own deadline and pass the caller's token through. Retry only connection errors, 408, 429 and 5xx, and only idempotent requests or a POST that carries an idempotency key. Wait a jittered, capped exponential delay, honour Retry-After, and stop when attempts or the time budget run out.

ideas.idea: A role says what kind of user someone is; whether they may touch this object needs the object: load it, check its tenant, then apply role and ownership rules.
ideas.why: Endpoint-level role checks let an approver of one tenant act on another tenant's records by changing the id, and a 403 for foreign ids confirms they exist.
ideas.prompt: An invoice endpoint has [Authorize(Roles = "approver")] and nothing else. A pen test approves another company's invoice by editing the id, and a clerk approves their own invoice after being made an approver. What do you change?
ideas.answer: Load the invoice and compare its tenant with the caller's tenant claim before anything else, answering 404 for another tenant just as for a missing id. Then require the approver role and a different creator, ideally as a resource-based policy called through IAuthorizationService, and filter list queries by tenant inside the query.

ideas.idea: Log with message templates so values become searchable properties, carry a correlation id in a scope, and choose what goes in: never tokens, passwords, bodies or personal data.
ideas.why: A log line is copied into several systems and kept for months, so a secret in it leaks to everyone who can search the logs, and an interpolated line can be neither grouped nor queried.
ideas.prompt: An incident review finds bearer tokens and customer emails in the log store, and nobody can pull together the lines of one failing request. The code logs $"Request {body}" and every request header. What do you change?
ideas.answer: Switch to templates with named placeholders, open a scope with the correlation id in middleware, log an allow-listed set of headers and mark the rest as [Redacted], log the body's length instead of the body, then rotate the leaked tokens and purge those lines.

ideas.idea: Background work goes through a bounded queue to a worker that catches per job, tells shutdown from failure by the stopping token, and hands back what it cannot finish.
ideas.why: Fire-and-forget tasks lose their scope and vanish on deploy, an unbounded queue grows until memory runs out, and one escaped exception stops the whole host by default.
ideas.prompt: A checkout endpoint sends confirmation emails with Task.Run. After each deploy some emails never arrive, and one malformed address once took the whole service down. How do you restructure it?
ideas.answer: Write an email job to a bounded channel and return. A BackgroundService reads it, creates a scope per job, logs and skips a failing job, and ends only on the stopping token. On shutdown it completes the writer, drains until the deadline and puts unfinished jobs into an outbox table for retry.

ideas.idea: Publish DTOs, not entities, and pin one set of System.Text.Json options: names, unknown members, nulls, enums as names and the discriminator are all part of the contract.
ideas.why: Defaults differ between ASP.NET Core and a plain JsonSerializer call, so the same type can read silently as zeros, accept unknown fields, take any enum number and leak entity columns.
ideas.prompt: A partner reads your orders with a console tool. It receives status as 1, sometimes sees orderId come back as zero without complaint, and once saw a passwordHash field. What do you fix?
ideas.answer: Return an OrderDto mapped from the entity, never the entity. Share one options object built from the Web defaults, with a string enum converter that refuses integers, unmapped members disallowed, nulls left out and nullable annotations respected, and test the exact JSON of each DTO.
